781.event_title: The friendship of the Marquis de Lafayette and George Washington
781.event: In 1777 the nineteen-year-old Marquis de Lafayette defied King Louis XVI's order to remain in France, sailed to America to join the cause of independence and was made a major general by Congress. Wounded at the Battle of Brandywine in September 1777, he was treated by George Washington's own surgeon, and from then on the two men developed a bond that has been described as more like that of father and son than of commander and officer. Lafayette later returned to France to seek more support for the Americans and, in 1781, harried Cornwallis's army in Virginia before the allied victory at Yorktown.
781.explanation: A friendship formed in wartime became one of the Revolution's great assets, binding the American commander to a French nobleman who worked to win his own country's help for the cause.
781.tie_back: The kural asks what is as hard to win as friendship and what guards as surely against an enemy's efforts; Lafayette's rare loyalty became a real defence for Washington's cause.
781._accuracy_note: Good illustration of friendship as a protection against the enemy; the idea that such friendship is hard to win fits less directly.

782.event_title: Einstein and Michele Besso: from sounding board to collaborator
782.event: Albert Einstein's 1905 paper on special relativity famously acknowledged the help of his friend and colleague Michele Besso, who served as a sounding board for his ideas. In the following years the friendship grew into active collaboration: between June 1913 and early 1914 the two men worked together on a 54-page manuscript of calculations on the motion of Mercury's perihelion, written partly in Einstein's hand and partly in Besso's. In the same period Besso also acted as a go-between in Einstein's difficult family affairs.
782.explanation: Their relationship shows a friendship that kept deepening over the years, from conversation partner to working collaborator and family confidant.
782.tie_back: The kural compares friendship with the worthy to the crescent moon that grows fuller night by night, and Besso's friendship with Einstein grew steadily in depth.
782._accuracy_note: Shows only the waxing half of the kural's contrast; no waning friendship with a fool is involved.

783.event_title: The Inklings read their work aloud in Oxford
783.event: From about 1933, C. S. Lewis, J. R. R. Tolkien and a circle of Oxford friends met weekly, usually on Thursday evenings in Lewis's rooms at Magdalen College, to read aloud and criticise one another's writing in progress. The group heard and discussed early drafts of Tolkien's The Lord of the Rings and Lewis's The Great Divorce, and its members also gathered at the Eagle and Child pub. The Thursday meetings continued until the end of the 1940s.
783.explanation: Out of these repeated meetings came both lasting friendships and some of the most widely read books of the twentieth century.
783.tie_back: Valluvar says friendship with people of fine character is like a great book that gives more delight each time one returns to it, and for the Inklings friendship and the rereading of books were the same weekly pleasure.
783._accuracy_note: Strong fit: repeated companionship among good friends deepened through shared reading, which is the kural's own image.

784.event_title: Ezra Pound urges T. S. Eliot to cut The Waste Land
784.event: Before The Waste Land was published in 1922, T. S. Eliot submitted his drafts to his friend and fellow poet Ezra Pound, who had championed Eliot's work since they met in London in 1914. Pound urged Eliot to cut several long passages, among them a long section in heroic couplets imitating Pope, and Eliot accepted much of his advice, though not all of it. The drafts with Pound's markings were later found among the papers of the New York lawyer John Quinn and published in facsimile in 1971.
784.explanation: Pound's blunt criticism is widely credited with shaping a sprawling draft into one of the most influential poems of the twentieth century.
784.tie_back: The kural says friends are not only for laughing together but for stepping in first to rebuke one another when one goes too far, and Pound did exactly this, cutting away his friend's excesses.
784._accuracy_note: Partial fit: the rebuke concerned literary excess rather than moral wrongdoing, which is the kural's main concern.

785.event_title: Du Fu's lasting devotion to Li Bai after a brief companionship
785.event: In 744 the young poet Du Fu met the older and already celebrated Li Bai, probably in Luoyang, and the two travelled together in Henan and, in 745, in Shandong before parting at the end of that year. The standard chronology of Du Fu's life records no later meeting between them. Du Fu went on to write many poems to or about Li Bai, including one describing how his absent friend came to him in a dream.
785.explanation: Their friendship rested less on time spent together than on a deep mutual understanding of poetry and feeling, which Du Fu kept alive in verse for years.
785.tie_back: The kural says friendship needs neither frequent meetings nor long acquaintance, since shared feeling alone gives the full claim of friendship, and Du Fu's long remembrance of a companion of barely two years shows this.
785._accuracy_note: Strong fit: a brief acquaintance that became a deep and lasting friendship through shared feeling.

786.event_title: Montaigne's friendship with Etienne de La Boetie
786.event: Around 1559 Michel de Montaigne, then a member of the Parlement of Bordeaux, met Etienne de La Boetie, who also worked for the Parlement, and the two formed a deep friendship that lasted until La Boetie's death at the age of thirty-two in August 1563. Montaigne later oversaw the publication of several of his friend's works. In his essay Of Friendship he set this bond apart from ordinary friendships, which he called mere acquaintances, describing a friendship in which two souls are blended so completely that the seam joining them disappears.
786.explanation: Montaigne's essay made this friendship the classic European example of a bond rooted in the heart rather than in convenience or outward courtesy.
786.tie_back: The kural says friendship that only makes the face smile is not friendship, while friendship that makes the heart smile is, and Montaigne drew the same line between ordinary acquaintance and what he shared with La Boetie.
786._accuracy_note: Strong fit on the contrast between outward and heartfelt friendship, drawn by Montaigne himself.

787.event_title: Friedrich Engels supports Karl Marx for decades
787.place: Manchester and London, England, United Kingdom
787.event: Friedrich Engels, the son of a cotton manufacturer, first met Karl Marx in 1842 and renewed the contact in 1844. While Marx lived in London and wrote, Engels worked for many years in his family's firm in Manchester and sent him money, support that Smithsonian magazine describes as lasting nearly forty years and beginning even before Engels himself was well off. After Marx died in 1883, Engels devoted much of his remaining time to publishing his friend's unfinished work.
787.explanation: Engels kept his friend and his family afloat through long years of poverty and then preserved his friend's writings after his death.
787.tie_back: The kural says friendship keeps a friend from ruin, helps him along his path and shares his hardship when it comes, and Engels did all of this for Marx over four decades.
787._accuracy_note: Strong on rescuing a friend from ruin and sharing his burdens; the entry concerns the personal friendship, not the politics of either man.

788.event_title: Joshua Speed offers Abraham Lincoln a place to sleep
788.event: On 15 April 1837 Abraham Lincoln, newly arrived in Springfield to practise law, walked into Joshua Speed's store and asked the price of bedding, but found he could not afford it and asked for credit. Speed, taken with the stranger, at once offered to share his own living quarters above the store, and Lincoln accepted on the spot. The two shared those quarters for several years and became close and lasting friends.
788.explanation: A moment of spontaneous generosity began one of the most important friendships of Lincoln's life, one that later helped him through a period of deep despair.
788.tie_back: The kural compares friendship to the hand that flies to catch a slipping garment without being asked, and Speed solved a stranger's embarrassment immediately, before Lincoln could even finish asking for credit.
788._accuracy_note: Strong on instant, unasked help; the two were strangers at that moment, so it shows the start of a friendship rather than help between old friends.

789.event_title: Anne Sullivan's decades of support for Helen Keller
789.place: Tuscumbia, Alabama, and elsewhere in the United States
789.event: On 3 March 1887 Anne Sullivan, a former pupil of the Perkins Institution, arrived at the Keller home in Tuscumbia to teach six-year-old Helen Keller, who could neither see nor hear, by spelling words into her hand. Sullivan stayed with Keller long after the famous breakthrough at the water pump, and when Keller entered Radcliffe College in 1900 Sullivan spelled out all the lectures and unbrailled texts for her, at great cost to her own weak eyesight. Keller graduated with honours in 1904, and Sullivan remained her interpreter and constant companion for decades afterwards.
789.explanation: Sullivan's steady, many-sided support made possible Keller's education and her later life as an author and public figure.
789.tie_back: The kural places friendship on its throne when it stands firm without wavering and holds the other up in every way it can, and Sullivan's decades of unwavering support are as complete an example as history offers.
789._accuracy_note: Very strong on constancy and support in every way; the relationship began as teacher and pupil rather than as a friendship between equals.

790.event_title: Hardy and Littlewood agree never to keep score
790.event: From about 1911 the Cambridge mathematicians G. H. Hardy and J. E. Littlewood began a collaboration that lasted some 35 years. According to their colleague Harald Bohr, they agreed on a set of informal rules, which Mary Cartwright believed date from 1912: neither was obliged to answer or even read the other's letters, it did not matter whether what they wrote to each other was right or wrong, and every joint paper would carry both names regardless of whether one of them had contributed anything to it.
790.explanation: By refusing to keep accounts of who did what, the two built one of the most productive partnerships in the history of mathematics.
790.tie_back: The kural warns that friends who keep count of what each is to the other cheapen their friendship, and Hardy and Littlewood made not keeping count a formal rule.
790._accuracy_note: The kural warns against measuring and advertising a friendship; this shows the opposite habit of refusing to tally contributions, a reasonable but indirect fit.
